rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: What is meant by doping of an intrinsic semiconductor ? Name the two types of atoms used for doping of Ge/Si.
rows.solution:
**Doping** is the deliberate addition of a small, controlled amount of a suitable impurity to a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor in order to raise its conductivity. The proportion is tiny — typically one impurity atom per \(10^{5}\) to \(10^{8}\) host atoms — yet it changes the conductivity by many orders of magnitude, because it supplies carriers that need only a few hundredths of an electron-volt to be freed, instead of the full band gap.

The dopant must fit into the lattice without distorting it, which is why atoms of similar size to Ge or Si are used, drawn from the neighbouring groups.

**The two types of dopant atoms:**

**(i) Pentavalent atoms** — arsenic (As), antimony (Sb) or phosphorus (P). Four of their five valence electrons form covalent bonds with the host; the fifth is loosely bound and easily freed. These are **donors**, and the result is an **n-type** semiconductor in which electrons are the majority carriers.

**(ii) Trivalent atoms** — indium (In), boron (B) or aluminium (Al). With only three valence electrons, one bond is left incomplete, creating a vacancy that behaves as a mobile positive carrier. These are **acceptors**, and the result is a **p-type** semiconductor in which holes are the majority carriers.

The doped crystal remains electrically **neutral** throughout — doping does not add net charge, only mobile carriers, with the compensating charge fixed on the immobile dopant ion.

rows.subtopic: Atomic Masses and Composition of the Nucleus
rows.stem:
(i) Distinguish between isotopes and isobars.
(ii) Two nuclei have different mass numbers \(A_1\) and \(A_2\). Are these nuclei necessarily the isotopes of the same element ? Explain.
rows.solution:
**(i) Isotopes and isobars.**

**Isotopes** are nuclei with the **same atomic number \(Z\) but different mass numbers \(A\)** — the same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons. They are therefore the same chemical element, occupying one place in the periodic table, and are chemically almost indistinguishable. Examples: \({}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\), \({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\), \({}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\).

**Isobars** are nuclei with the **same mass number \(A\) but different atomic numbers \(Z\)** — the same total number of nucleons, differently divided between protons and neutrons. They are different chemical elements with quite different properties. Examples: \({}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) and \({}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}\).

**(ii) Do different mass numbers imply isotopes of the same element?**

**No.** Different mass numbers \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) tell us only that the two nuclei contain different total numbers of nucleons. That says nothing about how those nucleons are divided.

To be **isotopes**, the two nuclei must additionally have the **same atomic number \(Z\)**. If their atomic numbers differ, they are nuclei of different elements altogether, and no relation of isotopy holds.

For instance, \({}^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) and \({}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) have different mass numbers and the same \(Z = 6\), so they *are* isotopes. But \({}^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) and \({}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N}\) also have different mass numbers, and are not isotopes of anything — they are carbon and nitrogen. The mass number alone is never sufficient; it is \(Z\) that identifies the element.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem:
(i) Name the factors on which photoelectric emission from a surface depends.
(ii) Define the term 'threshold frequency' for a photosensitive material.
rows.solution:
**(i) Factors on which photoelectric emission depends.**

- **The frequency of the incident radiation.** Emission occurs only if the frequency exceeds the threshold frequency \(\nu_0\) of the surface. Below it, no electron is emitted however intense or prolonged the illumination.
- **The intensity of the incident radiation.** Above threshold, the number of photoelectrons emitted per second — and hence the saturation photocurrent — is proportional to the intensity.
- **The nature of the emitting surface**, through its **work function** \(\phi_0\). A metal with a low work function, such as caesium, responds to visible light; one with a high work function, such as zinc, requires ultraviolet.

(The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons depends on frequency and work function only, never on intensity.)

**(ii) Threshold frequency.**

The threshold frequency of a photosensitive material is the **minimum frequency of incident radiation below which photoelectric emission does not occur at all**, however great the intensity.

It is related to the work function by

\(\phi_0 = h\nu_0\)

and it is a property of the material alone. At exactly \(\nu = \nu_0\) an electron is just freed, emerging with zero kinetic energy; above it, the surplus \(h(\nu - \nu_0)\) appears as the electron's maximum kinetic energy.

Its existence is the sharpest evidence for the quantum nature of light: on a wave picture, energy delivered continuously would eventually free an electron at any frequency, given enough time or brightness.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: Explain the formation of the barrier potential in a p-n junction.
rows.solution:
When a p-n junction is formed, the barrier potential appears of its own accord, before any external voltage is applied.

**The diffusion.** The p-side is rich in holes and the n-side rich in electrons, so across the junction there is a steep concentration gradient in both carriers. Electrons diffuse from the n-side into the p-side and holes from the p-side into the n-side, recombining as they arrive.

**The immobile charge left behind.** The dopant ions are fixed in the crystal lattice and cannot follow. An electron leaving the n-side strands a positively charged **donor ion** there; a hole leaving the p-side strands a negatively charged **acceptor ion**. A layer therefore builds up with **immobile positive charge on the n-side and immobile negative charge on the p-side** of the junction — the depletion region, emptied of mobile carriers.

**The resulting potential difference.** These two sheets of opposite fixed charge set up an electric field across the layer, directed from the n-side towards the p-side. A field across a distance means a **potential difference**, with the n-side at a higher potential than the p-side. This is the **barrier potential** \(V_b\).

**Why it stabilises.** The field it represents opposes the very diffusion that created it: any further electron trying to cross into the p-region must now climb a potential hill. As the layer widens the barrier strengthens, until diffusion is exactly balanced by the opposing drift of minority carriers. At equilibrium the net current is zero and the barrier stops growing.

Its magnitude is about \(0{\cdot}3\) V for germanium and \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon, and it is what a forward bias must overcome before the diode conducts appreciably. It cannot be measured directly with a voltmeter across an isolated diode, because equal and opposite contact potentials arise at the two metal terminals and cancel it exactly.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: State Bohr's postulate to explain stable orbits in a hydrogen atom. Prove that the speed with which the electron revolves in \(n^{th}\) orbit is proportional to \((1/n)\).
rows.solution:
**Bohr's postulate for stable orbits.**

An electron can revolve around the nucleus only in those orbits for which its **angular momentum is an integral multiple of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\)**:

\(m v_n r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

In these stationary states the electron does not radiate, contrary to what classical electromagnetism predicts for an accelerating charge — which is what makes the atom stable.

**Proving that \(v_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\).**

The electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the electron supplies the centripetal force:

\(\dfrac{m v_n^{2}}{r_n} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r_n^{2}}\)

which simplifies to

\(m v_n^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r_n} \qquad \text{...(1)}\)

From the quantisation postulate,

\(r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m v_n} \qquad \text{...(2)}\)

Substituting (2) into (1) to eliminate \(r_n\):

\(m v_n^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \times \dfrac{2\pi m v_n}{nh}\)

One factor of \(m v_n\) cancels from both sides:

\(v_n = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2\varepsilon_0 h}\cdot\dfrac{1}{n}\)

Everything outside the \(1/n\) is a combination of fundamental constants, so

\(v_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\)

as required.

The electron therefore moves **fastest in the innermost orbit** and slows as \(n\) grows. Putting \(n = 1\) gives \(v_1 = 2{\cdot}18 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), about \(c/137\) — the fine-structure constant, and the reason a non-relativistic treatment of hydrogen works as well as it does.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: Briefly explain how emf is generated in a solar cell. Draw its I-V characteristics.
rows.solution:
**How the emf is generated.**

A solar cell is a p-n junction with a very thin, transparent top layer so that light reaches the junction region. It is used with **no external bias**; the light itself does the work, through three processes in sequence.

**(i) Generation.** Photons of energy \(h\nu > E_g\) are absorbed in or very near the depletion region, each creating an **electron–hole pair**. The junction has to lie close to the illuminated surface, or the pairs form too far away to be collected.

**(ii) Separation.** The depletion region already carries the built-in field, directed from the n-side to the p-side. It sweeps the two carriers apart before they can recombine — **electrons to the n-side, holes to the p-side**. This is the decisive step: without a field to separate them, the pair would simply recombine and the energy would be lost as heat.

**(iii) Collection.** Electrons arriving on the n-side are gathered by the front contact and holes arriving on the p-side by the back contact.

Charge therefore accumulates with the **p-side positive and the n-side negative**, and this separation is the photovoltage across the terminals.

**The I–V characteristic.**

The curve is drawn in the **fourth quadrant** — positive voltage with negative current — which is the signature of a device *delivering* power rather than consuming it. Two points label it:

- \(I_{SC}\), the **short-circuit current**, where the curve meets the current axis at \(V = 0\). It is proportional to the light intensity.
- \(V_{OC}\), the **open-circuit voltage**, where the curve meets the voltage axis at \(I = 0\). It is close to, but always less than, the band gap expressed in volts.

Between the two the curve bends over, and the operating point delivering maximum power is the one where the rectangle under the curve has the greatest area.

rows.stem:
A narrow beam of protons, each having 4.1 MeV energy is approaching a sheet of lead \((Z = 82)\). Calculate :
(i) the speed of a proton in the beam, and
(ii) the distance of its closest approach
rows.solution:
**(i) Speed of a proton.**

Converting the energy: \(4{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 4{\cdot}1 \times 10^{6} \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 6{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-13}\) J.

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = K \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}}\)

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 6{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-13}}{1{\cdot}673 \times 10^{-27}}} = \sqrt{7{\cdot}84 \times 10^{14}}\)

\(v = 2{\cdot}8 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

(About 9% of the speed of light, so a non-relativistic treatment is adequate here.)

**(ii) Distance of closest approach.**

At closest approach the proton has stopped, and all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy. The proton carries charge \(e\) and the lead nucleus \(Ze\) with \(Z = 82\):

\(K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{d} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{K}\)

\(d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 82 \times (1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19})^{2}}{6{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-13}}\)

\(d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 82 \times 2{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-38}}{6{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-13}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}89 \times 10^{-26}}{6{\cdot}56 \times 10^{-13}}\)

\(d = 2{\cdot}88 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{m}\)

The projectile here is a **proton**, not an alpha particle, so the numerator carries \(Ze^{2}\) rather than \(2Ze^{2}\) — the commonest slip in this calculation, and worth an extra look since the alpha-particle version is the one usually memorised.

The result is instructive: \(2{\cdot}88 \times 10^{-14}\) m is about four times the radius of a lead nucleus (\(\sim\!7 \times 10^{-15}\) m). The proton therefore never reaches the nucleus, and the whole encounter is governed by the Coulomb force alone — which is exactly the condition under which Rutherford's scattering formula holds.

rows.stem:
In a diffraction pattern due to a single slit, how will the angular width of central maximum change, if
(i) Orange light is used in place of green light,
(ii) the screen is moved closer to the slit,
(iii) the slit width is decreased ?
Justify your answer in each case.
rows.solution:
The angular width of the central maximum in single-slit diffraction is

\(2\theta = \dfrac{2\lambda}{a}\)

where \(a\) is the slit width. Note what does **not** appear: the screen distance \(D\).

**(i) Orange light in place of green — the angular width increases.**

Orange light has the longer wavelength of the two (about 600 nm against 550 nm). Since \(2\theta \propto \lambda\), a longer wavelength spreads the pattern out and the central maximum widens.

**(ii) Screen moved closer to the slit — no change.**

The angular width contains no \(D\), so moving the screen leaves it untouched. What does change is the **linear** width of the central band on the screen, \(2\lambda D/a\), which shrinks in proportion to \(D\). The pattern is a fixed set of directions; the screen merely intercepts it nearer, catching a smaller projection of the same angular spread.

**(iii) Slit width decreased — the angular width increases.**

Since \(2\theta \propto \dfrac{1}{a}\), narrowing the slit widens the central maximum. This is the counter-intuitive hallmark of diffraction: squeezing the light through a narrower aperture makes it spread *more*, not less.

The three cases separate two quantities that are easy to conflate. \(\lambda\) and \(a\) belong to the physics of the diffraction and set the angular pattern; \(D\) belongs only to the geometry of observation and scales what is seen without altering it. Taken to the limit, \(a \to \lambda\) gives \(\theta \to 90^\circ\) and the light spreads into the whole forward hemisphere — which is why a very narrow slit behaves almost as a point source of secondary wavelets.

rows.stem:
(a) Write two necessary conditions for total internal reflection.
(b) Two prisms ABC and DBC are arranged as shown in figure. The critical angles for the two prisms with respect to air are \(41.1^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\) respectively. Trace the path of the ray through the combination.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says 'as shown in figure' and states no geometry in words. The drawing carries the vertex labels A, B, C and D, a 45 degree angle at A, 60 degree angles at B and D, a right-angle mark on face AB where a horizontal ray enters from the left, and the shared face BC dividing the upper prism ABC from the lower prism DBC. Describing labelling and layout only: the path of the ray through the combination is what the question asks the student to trace and is NOT drawn on the question paper. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
**(a) Two necessary conditions for total internal reflection.**

**(i)** The light must travel from an **optically denser medium into a rarer one** — from higher refractive index to lower.

**(ii)** The **angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle** for that pair of media, where \(\sin i_c = n_{\text{rarer}}/n_{\text{denser}}\).

**(b) Tracing the ray through the two prisms.**

From the figure, prism ABC has \(\angle A = 45^\circ\) with AB vertical, and prism DBC below it is equilateral, with \(\angle B = \angle D = 60^\circ\). The critical angles are \(41{\cdot}1^\circ\) for ABC and \(45^\circ\) for DBC.

**Step 1 — at face AB.** The ray arrives **normally**, so it enters without bending and travels horizontally into ABC.

**Step 2 — at face AC.** Face AC makes \(45^\circ\) with AB, so the horizontal ray meets it at an angle of incidence of \(45^\circ\).

\(45^\circ > 41{\cdot}1^\circ\), the critical angle for this prism, so the ray is **totally internally reflected**. Reflection off a surface inclined at \(45^\circ\) turns the horizontal ray through \(90^\circ\), sending it **vertically downwards**.

**Step 3 — through face BC.** BC is horizontal and the ray is vertical, so it crosses into the lower prism at **normal incidence**, undeviated.

**Step 4 — at face BD.** In the equilateral prism, BD makes \(60^\circ\) with the horizontal BC, so the vertical ray meets BD at an angle of incidence of \(60^\circ\).

\(60^\circ > 45^\circ\), the critical angle for DBC, so the ray is **totally internally reflected again**, now travelling down and to the right at \(30^\circ\) below the horizontal.

**Step 5 — at face DC.** That reflected direction is exactly along the normal to DC, so the ray **emerges normally**, without bending.

**The path in summary:** the ray enters undeviated, is totally internally reflected twice — once at AC and once at BD — and leaves through DC undeviated, emerging \(30^\circ\) below its original direction.

Both reflections are total, so essentially no light is lost at either surface. This is precisely why prisms rather than mirrors are used to fold light paths in binoculars and periscopes: a metallic mirror loses a few per cent at every bounce, while a totally internally reflecting face loses none.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem:
(a) An object is placed in front of a converging lens. Obtain the conditions under which the magnification produced by the lens is (i) negative and (ii) positive.
(b) A point object is placed at O in front of a glass sphere as shown in figure. Show the formation of image by the sphere.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the object distance exists ONLY in the drawing. It shows a point object O on a dashed horizontal axis running to a glass sphere of centre C and radius r, with the distance from O to the sphere marked 3r. The stem states no distance at all, so part (b) is unanswerable without it. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
**(a) When the magnification is negative, and when positive.**

For a lens the magnification is

\(m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{v}{u}\)

with the Cartesian convention, in which a real object always has \(u\) negative.

**(i) Negative magnification — the image is real and inverted.** This needs \(v\) and \(u\) to have opposite signs, so \(v\) must be **positive**: the image lies on the far side of the lens, where the light actually goes. From the lens equation, \(v > 0\) requires the object to be placed **beyond the focus**, \(\left|u\right| > f\).

**(ii) Positive magnification — the image is virtual and erect.** This needs \(v\) and \(u\) to have the same sign, so \(v\) must be **negative**: the image lies on the same side as the object. This happens when the object is placed **between the focus and the optical centre**, \(\left|u\right| < f\) — the configuration in which a converging lens is used as a simple magnifier.

The boundary is the focal point itself: an object exactly at F sends out parallel light and forms no image at any finite distance.

**(b) Image formation by the glass sphere.**

The sphere refracts the light **twice**, once at each spherical surface, and the image of the first refraction is the object for the second.

*At the first (near) surface.* Light from O, a distance \(3r\) away in air, meets a convex surface of radius \(r\). Refracting into the denser glass, the rays are bent towards the axis and converge more strongly than they would have. Because the object is comparatively far away, this first surface forms its image **beyond the far side of the sphere**.

*At the second (far) surface.* That image now serves as a **virtual object** for the second surface — the light is already converging towards a point past it. Refracting from glass back out into air, the rays are bent towards the axis once more, so they converge **sooner** than they otherwise would.

*The result.* The final image **I** is **real and inverted**, formed on the axis a short distance beyond the far surface of the sphere.

As an illustration, taking the usual \(\mu = 1{\cdot}5\): the first surface gives \(v_1 = 9r\) from the near face, which is \(7r\) beyond the far face; treating that as a virtual object for the second surface gives a final image about \(1{\cdot}4r\) beyond the sphere — just outside it, as the figure shows. (The refractive index is not stated in the question, so this is an illustration of the construction rather than a required number.)

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem:
An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. Find :
(i) the wavelength associated with
(ii) the momentum of and
(iii) the velocity required by, the electron.
rows.solution:
An electron starting from rest and accelerated through a potential difference \(V\) gains kinetic energy \(eV\).

**(i) Wavelength.**

Combining \(eV = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\) with \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\) gives the standard compact result

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}23}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{nm}\)

With \(V = 100\) V:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{1{\cdot}23}{\sqrt{100}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}23}{10} = 0{\cdot}123\ \mathrm{nm} = 1{\cdot}23\ \text{Å}\)

**(ii) Momentum.**

\(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{0{\cdot}123 \times 10^{-9}}\)

\(p = 5{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\)

**(iii) Velocity.**

\(v = \dfrac{p}{m} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-24}}{9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31}}\)

\(v = 5{\cdot}9 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

*Checking independently:* \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} \times 100}{9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31}}} = 5{\cdot}9 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which agrees.

The wavelength is worth pausing on: \(1{\cdot}23\) Å is comparable to the spacing between atoms in a crystal, which is exactly why a beam of 100 eV electrons diffracts from a crystal lattice. That is the Davisson–Germer experiment, and it is the direct experimental confirmation of de Broglie's hypothesis.

rows.stem:
In a Young's double slit experiment using light of wavelength 600 nm, the slit separation is 0.8 mm and the screen is kept 1.6 m from the plane of the slits. Calculate :
(i) the fringe width
(ii) the distance of (a) third minimum and (b) fifth maximum, from the central maximum.
rows.solution:
With \(\lambda = 600\ \mathrm{nm} = 600 \times 10^{-9}\) m, \(d = 0{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{mm} = 8 \times 10^{-4}\) m and \(D = 1{\cdot}6\) m:

**(i) Fringe width.**

\(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}6}{8 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{9{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-7}}{8 \times 10^{-4}}\)

\(\beta = 1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1{\cdot}2\ \text{mm}\)

**(ii)(a) Third minimum.**

Dark fringes sit midway between bright ones, at

\(x_n = \left(n - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\beta\)

For the third, \(n = 3\):

\(x_3 = \dfrac{5}{2}\beta = 2{\cdot}5 \times 1{\cdot}2 = 3\ \text{mm}\)

**(ii)(b) Fifth maximum.**

Bright fringes sit at whole multiples of the fringe width:

\(x_5 = 5\beta = 5 \times 1{\cdot}2 = 6\ \text{mm}\)

Once \(\beta\) is known both distances are simply counted off it, which is the point of computing the fringe width first. The two answers also confirm the structure of the pattern: the fifth bright fringe at 6 mm lies beyond the fifth dark fringe at \(4{\cdot}5\beta = 5{\cdot}4\) mm, and the two families interleave at half-fringe spacing all the way out.

(The marking scheme substitutes \(1{\cdot}2\) for \(D\) in its working, where the question gives \(1{\cdot}6\) m; its own answer of \(1{\cdot}2\) mm requires the correct \(1{\cdot}6\), so the printed numerator looks like the answer having bled into the substitution.)

rows.stem:
Electromagnetic waves of wavelengths \(\lambda_1\), \(\lambda_2\) and \(\lambda_3\) are used in radar systems, in water purifiers and in remote switches of TV, respectively.
(i) Identify the electromagnetic waves, and
(ii) Write one source of each of them.
rows.solution:
**(i) Identifying the three waves, and (ii) a source of each.**

**\(\lambda_1\) — radar systems: MICROWAVES.**

Wavelengths from about 1 mm to 1 m. They are short enough to be formed into a narrow beam by a modest dish yet long enough to penetrate cloud and rain, which is exactly what radar requires.

*Source:* a **magnetron**, or a klystron valve or Gunn diode — devices in which electrons are made to oscillate in a resonant cavity at microwave frequencies.

**\(\lambda_2\) — water purifiers: ULTRAVIOLET.**

Wavelengths from about 400 nm down to 1 nm. UV photons carry enough energy to damage the DNA of bacteria and viruses, killing them without adding any chemical to the water.

*Source:* a **high-voltage gas discharge tube**, typically a low-pressure mercury-vapour lamp, whose strong line at 254 nm is the germicidal wavelength. (The Sun is the natural source.)

**\(\lambda_3\) — remote switches of a TV: INFRARED.**

Wavelengths from about 700 nm to 1 mm. Infrared is invisible, so the signal is unobtrusive, and it is easily produced and detected by cheap semiconductor devices.

*Source:* **hot bodies and molecules** — any warm object radiates in the infrared. In a remote control specifically, an infrared-emitting **LED** made of gallium arsenide.

The three sit at widely separated points of the spectrum, and in each case the application follows from the photon energy. Microwave photons are far too feeble to interact chemically, which is what makes them safe to broadcast; infrared photons carry roughly the energy of molecular vibrations; ultraviolet photons carry enough to break chemical bonds, which is precisely why they sterilise.

rows.stem:
(i) State two conditions for two light sources to be coherent.
(ii) Give two points of difference between an interference pattern due to a double – slit and a diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
rows.solution:
**(i) Two conditions for two light sources to be coherent.**

- The two sources must emit waves of the **same wavelength** (hence the same frequency).
- They must maintain a **constant phase difference** — emitting either in phase, or with a difference that does not change with time.

Both are necessary. A frequency mismatch makes the phase difference drift steadily; a fluctuating phase makes the maxima wander. In either case the pattern sweeps across the screen faster than any detector can follow, and the time average is a uniform illumination with no fringes.

(Equal amplitude is **not** required. Unequal amplitudes still give interference, merely with imperfect contrast: the minima are no longer completely dark, since \(I_{\min} = \left(\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2}\right)^{2}\) vanishes only when the two intensities are equal.)

**(ii) Two differences between a double-slit interference pattern and a single-slit diffraction pattern.**

**Intensity of the bright bands.** In **interference** all the bright fringes have **nearly the same intensity**, each being a full constructive superposition of two equal beams. In **diffraction** the central maximum is overwhelmingly the brightest and the intensity of the secondary maxima **falls off rapidly** on either side — the first is only about 4·7% of the central peak, the second about 1·7%.

**Width of the bands.** In **interference** all the fringes are of the **same width** \(\beta = \lambda D/d\), evenly spaced across the pattern. In **diffraction** the fringes are **not all the same width**: the central maximum is **twice as wide** as any of the secondary maxima beyond it.

(A third difference worth knowing: interference arises from the superposition of light from two *separate* wavefronts, diffraction from the superposition of secondary wavelets originating within a *single* wavefront. The fringe spacings also depend on different lengths — the slit *separation* \(d\) for interference, the slit *width* \(a\) for diffraction.)

rows.stem: In a compound microscope the images formed by the objective and the eye-piece are respectively
rows.context: A compound microscope consists of two converging lenses. One of them, of smaller aperture and smaller focal length is called objective and the other of slightly larger aperture and slightly larger focal length is called eye-piece. Both the lenses are fitted in a tube with an arrangement to vary the distance between them. A tiny object is placed in front of the objective at a distance slightly greater than its focal length. The objective produces the image of the object which acts as an object for the eye-piece. The eye piece, in turn produces the final magnified image.
rows.solution:
In a compound microscope the two lenses do different jobs, and the images they form differ in kind.

**The objective** receives light from an object placed just **beyond its focus**. A converging lens with the object beyond F forms a **real**, inverted and magnified image, which is formed inside the tube and is where the light actually converges.

**The eyepiece** receives that intermediate image, positioned just **inside its own focal length**, and so acts as a simple magnifier. A converging lens with the object inside F forms a **virtual**, erect and magnified image — erect relative to the intermediate image, hence inverted relative to the original object.

So the images are **real, virtual** respectively — option (B).

The sequence is forced by the design. The objective must form a real image, or there would be nothing for the eyepiece to work on; and the eyepiece must form a virtual one, since the final image has to be at a comfortable viewing distance on the observer's side of the lens rather than projected onto a screen. The same two-stage arrangement, with the same real-then-virtual sequence, appears in the astronomical telescope.

rows.stem: The magnification due to a compound microscope does not depend upon

Both the lenses are fitted in a tube with an arrangement to vary the distance between them. A tiny object is placed in front of the objective at a distance slightly greater than its focal length. The objective produces the image of the object which acts as an object for the eye-piece. The eye piece, in turn produces the final magnified image.

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.text: the colour of the light used

rows.stem: Which of the following is not correct in the context of a compound microscope ?
rows.context: A compound microscope consists of two converging lenses. One of them, of smaller aperture and smaller focal length is called objective and the other of slightly larger aperture and slightly larger focal length is called eye-piece. Both the lenses are fitted in a tube with an arrangement to vary the distance between them. A tiny object is placed in front of the objective at a distance slightly greater than its focal length. The objective produces the image of the object which acts as an object for the eye-piece. The eye piece, in turn produces the final magnified image.

options.label: A
options.text: Both the lenses are of short focal lengths.

options.label: B
options.text: The magnifying power increases by decreasing the focal lengths of the two lenses.

options.label: C
options.text: The distance between the two lenses is more than (fo + fe).

options.label: D
options.text: The microscope can be used as a telescope by interchanging the two lenses.

rows.solution:
Taking the four statements in turn:

**(A) Both lenses are of short focal length — correct.** Since \(m \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)\), both focal lengths sit in denominators, so high magnification requires both to be small.

**(B) The magnifying power increases as the focal lengths decrease — correct**, for the same reason.

**(C) The distance between the lenses exceeds \((f_o + f_e)\) — correct.** The object sits just beyond \(f_o\), so its real image forms at \(v_o > f_o\); with the final image at infinity the eyepiece must then be \(f_e\) beyond that image, making the separation \(v_o + f_e > f_o + f_e\).

**(D) The microscope can be used as a telescope by interchanging the two lenses — not correct.**

Interchanging them cannot produce a telescope. A telescope requires a **long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece**, since its magnifying power is \(f_o/f_e\) — the opposite arrangement to a microscope. Both lenses of a microscope are short-focus, so swapping them merely exchanges one short focal length for another and yields a magnification close to 1. There is no long-focus lens anywhere in the instrument to serve as a telescope objective.

The answer is (D).

Statement (C) is the one most often misjudged: it is tempting to assume the tube length is exactly \(f_o + f_e\), but that holds for a **telescope** in normal adjustment, where the objective's image lies in its focal plane because the object is at infinity. In a microscope the object is at a finite distance just beyond F, so the intermediate image forms well beyond the focal plane.

rows.stem: A compound microscope consists of an objective of 10X and an eye-piece of 20X. The magnification due to the microscope would be
rows.context: A compound microscope consists of two converging lenses. One of them, of smaller aperture and smaller focal length is called objective and the other of slightly larger aperture and slightly larger focal length is called eye-piece. Both the lenses are fitted in a tube with an arrangement to vary the distance between them. A tiny object is placed in front of the objective at a distance slightly greater than its focal length. The objective produces the image of the object which acts as an object for the eye-piece. The eye piece, in turn produces the final magnified image.
rows.solution:
The magnification of a compound microscope is the **product** of the two stages, not their sum:

\(m = m_o \times m_e\)

A lens marked "10X" contributes a factor of 10, and one marked "20X" a factor of 20:

\(m = 10 \times 20 = 200\)

The answer is (D).

Option (C), 30, is what the sum would give, and it is the distractor the question is built around. The reason the contributions multiply is that the two stages act in sequence: the objective enlarges the object by a factor of 10, and the eyepiece then enlarges *that already enlarged image* by a further factor of 20. Each stage works on the output of the previous one, so the factors compound.

The same reasoning fixes the sign in the full expression \(m = \dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)\), and it is why a modest pair of lenses can reach magnifications of several hundred.

rows.stem: The focal lengths of objective and eye-piece of a compound microscope are 1.2 cm and 3.0 cm respectively. The object is placed at a distance of 1.25 cm from the objective. If the final image is formed at infinity, the magnifying power of the microscope would be
rows.context: A compound microscope consists of two converging lenses. One of them, of smaller aperture and smaller focal length is called objective and the other of slightly larger aperture and slightly larger focal length is called eye-piece. Both the lenses are fitted in a tube with an arrangement to vary the distance between them. A tiny object is placed in front of the objective at a distance slightly greater than its focal length. The objective produces the image of the object which acts as an object for the eye-piece. The eye piece, in turn produces the final magnified image.
rows.solution:
Work the two stages in turn, then multiply.

**The objective.** With \(f_o = 1{\cdot}2\) cm and the object at \(u_o = -1{\cdot}25\) cm:

\(\dfrac{1}{v_o} - \dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{f_o}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}2} + \dfrac{1}{(-1{\cdot}25)} = 0{\cdot}8333 - 0{\cdot}8 = 0{\cdot}0333\)

\(v_o = 30\ \text{cm}\)

so the objective's magnification is

\(m_o = \left|\dfrac{v_o}{u_o}\right| = \dfrac{30}{1{\cdot}25} = 24\)

**The eyepiece.** The final image is at infinity, so the eyepiece works in normal adjustment as a simple magnifier:

\(m_e = \dfrac{D}{f_e} = \dfrac{25}{3} = 8{\cdot}33\)

**Total:**

\(m = m_o \times m_e = 24 \times \dfrac{25}{3} = 200\)

The answer is (C).

The object distance \(1{\cdot}25\) cm is only a whisker beyond the focal length \(1{\cdot}2\) cm, and that small margin is what produces the large \(v_o = 30\) cm and hence the factor of 24. This is the design principle of the objective: placing the object *just* outside the focus is what buys the magnification, and it is also why focusing a microscope is so delicate — a movement of a few hundredths of a millimetre changes the image distance by centimetres.
